thread.title: CITIZEN COLUMNIST: It’s your money: Invest it yourself!

author: Tom Dorsel Citizen Columnist
title: CITIZEN COLUMNIST: It’s your money: Invest it yourself!
text:
Save
A turbulent stock market might be the perfect laboratory for learning about investing.
Experts don’t have a corner on this enterprise. No one knows for sure what the stock market will do next week or which stocks are the best to buy. So, why not give it a shot yourself with a little money you can afford to lose?
At the very least, your new learning will help you converse more intelligently with your financial adviser. A classroom experiment
In a former life at Francis Marion, I designed an undergraduate psychology course called “Family Life.” It addressed everything family from finding a mate and marriage, to giving birth and raising children, to establishing careers and managing finances, as well as life transitions, aging, death and dying.
Even though I am just a psychologist and not a professional financial adviser, one fun part of the course was an exercise in family investing that ran concurrent with the four-month course. I gave the students my best shot at some preliminary ideas on picking stocks and then awarded them three extra-credit points upfront as their trial currency for investing in the stock market.
Once they picked their stock, they could add to their extra-credit points if their stock performed well, lose all of their extra-credit points if their stock tanked, or they could even stick their extra-credit points under a mattress, if they were afraid to invest. However, if they did the latter, they only got to keep one of the extra points at the end of the semester, since the other two eroded away with inflation, just like money would under a mattress. The basics
>> What are stocks? Basically, a company sells itself to the public by issuing shares of stock that people buy at a price that the company initially establishes. From that point on, the new public owners trade these shares back and forth through stock exchanges (e.g., New York Stock Exchange, NASDAQ, etc.).
The upshot is that you buy shares of stock and can sell them pretty much anytime you want, the cash going back into your account for you to buy other stocks as opportunities arise.
>> Researching stocks. All stocks have symbols (e.g., Apple is AAPL, Starbucks is SBUX, Kohls is KSS). When you go on a financial website (e.g., Yahoo, Finance), you will find a search box where you can type in the name of a company or its symbol. Then a page for that company will appear with links to relevant investing information.
>> Capital gains. Every stock has a value (e.g., $10, $30, $50) per share that can go up or down each day. You buy a stock at its present dollar value, and when that dollar value goes up, you have a “capital gain” – your invested money (i.e., capital) is gaining money for you. Of course, the number also can go down, and you lose money for the moment. I say “for the moment,” because a stock can go up and down considerably in a matter of days, but the money you lose or make isn’t determined until you sell the stock.
>> Dividends. The other way to make money from a stock is by receiving the company’s dividends. To entice people to buy their stock, companies often give out a little money (dividends), usually quarterly, for each share of stock.
Similar to interest in a bank account, you might get a dividend equal to an annual rate of, say, 3 percent of the value of your stock. In this way, shareholders benefit in the profitability of a company without having to sell their shares to get their capital gains. Considerations when researching a stock
>> 1. Quality of the company (management, reputation, the future of its product).
>> 2. Price range of the company’s stock (buy low, sell high is the old adage).
>> 3. Reasons for the company’s stock price being down (business cycle, the industry or bad news regarding the company).
>> 4. Earnings of the company should be increasing annually (growth).
>> 5. P/E ratio (the company’s P rice in relation to its E arnings) – Lower P/E ratios are better, suggesting the company’s stock price is low relative to the company’s favorable earnings).
>> 6. PEG ratio (the company’s P/E ratio in relation to its G rowth) – Again, a lower ratio is better, representing a desirable low P/E ratio in a company that is exhibiting high growth).
>> 7. Dividend should be at a reasonable current amount and increasing annually.
>> 8. Yearly earnings per share are at least as high as the dividend (meaning the company can afford to keep paying its dividend).
>> 9. 12-month price target (the projected price that analysts think the stock will achieve in the next year).
>> 10. Debt (low debt means that the company can use its earnings to grow rather than to pay interest payments. It also means the company is not likely to go out of business in an economic downturn.)
All of these factors are ones you can learn more about from a financial website tutorial. At the very least, this list can get you started in searching for stocks that get good marks. Buying and selling stock
First, open an account with a traditional brokerage house (e.g., Morgan/Stanley, Wells Fargo Advisors, Merrill-Lynch, etc.) or with an online discount broker (e.g., TD Ameritrade, Fidelity, Charles Schwab, etc.). With the traditional broker, you will get advice, but you will pay more money for each buy and sell order (called a “trade”). With the online discount broker, you get little or no advice but pay much less for trades.
In both cases you can trade stocks over the telephone with the help of a broker or trade online using the brokerage houses’ websites. Strategic considerations
>> Only invest money you don’t need for near-term purposes and can otherwise afford to lose. This is gambling – calculated, but still a gamble!
>> Don’t expect to be lucky enough to buy at the precise bottom or sell at the precise top of a stock’s range. Somewhere in the vicinity of each is good enough.
>> Set target prices to buy and sell and then re-evaluate when the stocks hit those prices. If nothing has happened to change your mind, then make your move and don’t look back second-guessing yourself.
>> Buy reasonably priced, high-quality companies that you can hold for the long term, if necessary. Quality companies with solid financials generally increase in value over time.
>> Just because you learn about the stock market does not mean you have to invest immediately. The current high-priced market might not be the time to put your skin in the game. But a substantial pullback at some point might be a rare opportunity. In the meantime you will be watching and learning. Classroom results
After some understandable, initial hesitancy, 95 percent or so of the students saw how manageable self-investing was and dived in (using their) head first. And the few who dived under-the-mattress, oh, well, they got their one point, along with some suggested reading – Matthew 25:14–30. Remember, Matthew was a tax collector, so he probably liked this parable very much! Dr. Tom Dorsel is a resident-emeritus of Florence, now living on Hilton Head Island and serving as a “foreign correspondent” to the Morning News. He can be reached through his website, Dorsel.com .
